prompt: Retrieve a list of all flights and their corresponding ticket information. Ensure that flights without tickets are also included in the result. The output should display flight_id, flight_number, and ticket_id, ordered by flight_id.
reference_solution_sql:
SELECT f.id AS flight_id, f.flight_number, t.id AS ticket_id
FROM flights f
LEFT JOIN tickets t ON f.id = t.flight_id
ORDER BY f.id;

hints.hint: You want to show all flights regardless of ticket status. What type of join allows this?
Consider using a LEFT JOIN to include all rows from the flights table.
Make sure to order the results by flight_id after performing the LEFT JOIN.

FROM flights f
LEFT JOIN tickets t ON f.id = t.flight_id
ORDER BY f.id;

solution_steps.what_it_does: Start by selecting from the flights table, since you want to include all flights.
solution_steps.sql_snippet: FROM flights f
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: Postgres reads the flights table first and treats each flight as a potential result.

solution_steps.title: Join with the tickets table
solution_steps.what_it_does: Use LEFT JOIN to include ticket information associated with each flight.
solution_steps.sql_snippet: LEFT JOIN tickets t ON f.id = t.flight_id
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: Postgres matches each flight with its tickets, keeping all flights in the result even if no tickets exist.

solution_steps.title: Order the results
solution_steps.what_it_does: Sort the final output by flight_id for clarity.
solution_steps.sql_snippet: ORDER BY f.id
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: Postgres organizes the result set by the flight_id, ensuring that the output is in ascending order.

solution_summary: A LEFT JOIN between flights and tickets ensures all flights are displayed, even those without tickets, ordered by flight_id.

explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps all records from the flights table and matches ticket records wherever available. If there are no tickets for a flight, ticket_id will be NULL, ensuring all flights are reported, even those without tickets.

prompt: Find the total number of tickets for each flight, including those flights that have no tickets sold. Display flight_number and ticket_count, ordered by ticket_count in descending order.
reference_solution_sql:
SELECT f.flight_number, COUNT(t.id) AS ticket_count
FROM flights f
LEFT JOIN tickets t ON f.id = t.flight_id
GROUP BY f.flight_number
ORDER BY ticket_count DESC;

Use COUNT to aggregate ticket counts while ensuring flights without tickets are included.

FROM flights f
LEFT JOIN tickets t ON f.id = t.flight_id
GROUP BY f.flight_number
ORDER BY ticket_count DESC;

solution_steps.sql_snippet: FROM warehouses w
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: Postgres scans the warehouses table to gather base rows.

solution_steps.title: Left join with conditions
solution_steps.what_it_does: LEFT JOIN shipments while applying a condition on shipment_date.
solution_steps.sql_snippet: LEFT JOIN shipments s ON s.warehouse_id = w.id AND s.shipment_date > '2024-01-01'
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: Postgres matches shipments to warehouses, applying the condition to filter the joined records.

solution_steps.title: Count filtered shipments
solution_steps.what_it_does: COUNT aggregates the number of shipments for each warehouse after the date filter.
solution_steps.sql_snippet:
COUNT(s.id) AS count_of_shipments
GROUP BY w.id
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: Postgres counts the number of valid shipment records per warehouse based on the JOIN condition.

solution_steps.title: Order the output
solution_steps.what_it_does: ORDER BY organizes the results by warehouse name.
solution_steps.sql_snippet: ORDER BY w.name
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: Postgres sorts the final result set in ascending order by warehouse name.

solution_summary: A LEFT JOIN with a condition allows for counting shipments after a certain date while including all warehouses.
solution_final_thought: Incorporating conditions in LEFT JOINs provides flexibility in counting and filtering related records.
explanation: The LEFT JOIN with a condition on shipment_date allows for counting only those shipments that occurred after '2024-01-01'. Warehouses without relevant shipments still appear with a count of zero, ensuring comprehensive results.

prompt: List all warehouses with the number of shipments made in January 2024. Include warehouses with zero shipments. Return warehouse_name, january_shipments ordered by warehouse_name.
reference_solution_sql:
SELECT w.name AS warehouse_name, COUNT(s.id) AS january_shipments
FROM warehouses w
LEFT JOIN shipments s ON s.warehouse_id = w.id AND s.shipment_date >= '2024-01-01' AND s.shipment_date < '2024-02-01'
GROUP BY w.id
ORDER BY w.name;

hints.hint: You want to count shipments specifically for January 2024.
Use a LEFT JOIN with a condition for the date range to include all warehouses.
Include the date conditions in the LEFT JOIN and count the shipments per warehouse.

GROUP BY w.id
ORDER BY w.name;

prompt: Retrieve a list of all artists along with their albums. Include artists that do not have any albums, returning artist_id, artist_name, and album_name (use NULL for albums without a name).

hints.hint: You want to include all artists, even those without albums. What join type will help?
Think about how to join the artists table with the albums table. Use LEFT JOIN to include all records from artists.
Use LEFT JOIN on artists to albums, selecting artist details and album titles. Don't forget to alias your columns!

solution_steps.title: Select from artists
solution_steps.what_it_does: Begin the query from the artists table to ensure all artists are included in the result.
solution_steps.sql_snippet: FROM artists a
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: Postgres starts with the artists table and selects each artist as a candidate for the result.

solution_steps.title: Join albums with LEFT JOIN
solution_steps.what_it_does: Perform a LEFT JOIN to include albums that correspond to each artist while retaining those without albums.
solution_steps.sql_snippet: LEFT JOIN albums al ON a.id = al.artist_id
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: For each artist, Postgres looks for matching album records. If no match exists, it still includes the artist with NULL for album details.

solution_steps.title: Select desired columns
solution_steps.what_it_does: Select the specific columns needed for the output, including aliases for clarity.
solution_steps.sql_snippet: SELECT a.id AS artist_id, a.name AS artist_name, al.title AS album_name
solution_steps.how_postgres_reads_it: Postgres retrieves the specified columns from the joined tables, using the aliases for the final output.

solution_summary: A LEFT JOIN between artists and albums to ensure all artists are listed, regardless of whether they have albums.
solution_final_thought: LEFT JOIN allows you to include all records from the left table, even those without matches in the right table.
explanation: The LEFT JOIN ensures that all artists are included in the result set, even if they have no corresponding albums, which are represented as NULL in the output. This is crucial for reporting scenarios where you want to show all entities, regardless of their relationships.
